Supreme Court sides with Tennessee to allow its first execution of a woman in 200 years
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that Tennessee could proceed with its first execution of a woman in 200 years, clearing the way for Christa Pike to be put to death by lethal injection for murdering a schoolmate as an 18-year-old three decades ago.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement to Reuters afterwards that it planned “to move forward with the execution today.”
ADVERTISING
Pike, 50, whose clemency petition highlighting childhood trauma and sexual abuse was denied by Governor Bill Lee on Monday, would also be the only person in the modern era of U.S. capital punishment to be executed in Tennessee for a crime committed as a teenager.
In an order decided by its 6-3 conservative majority, the Supreme Court lifted a stay of execution that was granted by a three-judge panel of the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals one hour before Pike had been scheduled to be put to death.
The appellate panel voted 2-1 to order a “short stay” to allow time to weigh Pike’s claim that evidence of her childhood sexual abuse was not adequately considered during her sentencing.
But the Tennessee attorney general’s office immediately asked the U.S. Supreme Court to vacate the stay. And the high court’s decision siding with Tennessee marked the final word on whether the execution was permitted to go forward before her death warrant expires at midnight CDT.
The state did not give a precise new time frame for the execution, which was set to take place at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, the state capital.
If the state were to run out of time to conduct the execution, it would need to obtain a new warrant from the Tennessee Supreme Court, according to Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center.
Pike was 18 in January 1995 when she, a 17-year-old boyfriend and a third companion lured 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate at their Knoxville Job Corps vocational center, into a wooded area where they tortured and killed her.
The grisly nature of the slaying, which involved the perpetrators carving the shape of a pentagram in the victim’s chest and taking a chunk of her skull as a souvenir of the carnage, drew intense media coverage at the time.
Trial testimony indicated that Pike viewed Slemmer as a rival for the affections of her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp.
Pike and Shipp both were convicted of first-degree murder. Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Their co-defendant, Shadolla Peterson, who was 18 at the time of the murder and acted as a lookout for the other two, testified for the prosecution and received probation.

The U.S. Supreme Court has cleared the way for Tennessee to move forward with the execution of Christa Gail Pike after a federal appeals court issued an eleventh-hour stay.
The high court vacated the Sixth Circuit’s order Wednesday evening, removing the legal barrier that had halted the execution only hours earlier.
The ruling does not itself confirm that the lethal injection has been completed. It restores Tennessee’s authority to proceed under the active death warrant.
The first report captured the immediate result and the three-justice dissent.
BREAKING: The Supreme Court has cleared the way for Tennessee to execute Christa Pike, vacating a stay of execution issued by the Sixth Circuit earlier today. Justice Sotomayor dissented, joined by Kagan and Jackson. pic.twitter.com/GhAy0I2syS
— SCOTUS Wire (@scotus_wire) September 30, 2026
The legal fight moved with extraordinary speed.
Pike’s lawyers had already asked the Supreme Court to stop the execution in a separate case. The Court denied that request and her petition for review on Tuesday.
Then, on Wednesday morning, the Sixth Circuit voted 2-1 to impose a short stay while it considered whether Pike’s claims about childhood sexual abuse had received adequate consideration during sentencing.
Tennessee immediately returned to the Supreme Court and asked the justices to vacate that stay.
The U.S. Supreme Court docket shows Tennessee filed emergency application 26A428 on September 30 in the name of prison warden Kenneth Nelsen.
The application came from the Sixth Circuit case numbered 26-5864. Pike filed her response the same day, and Tennessee filed a reply as the state pressed for a decision before its death warrant expired.
The docket identifies Justice Brett Kavanaugh as the justice who received the emergency application. The matter was then presented to the full Court, which vacated the lower court’s stay.
That sequence followed Tuesday’s denial in Pike’s separate application 26A414, which challenged the death sentence through the Tennessee court system. The two proceedings show how the case moved through overlapping state and federal channels in its final hours.
The Supreme Court’s order drew dissents from Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson.
The history attached to the ruling made it one of Tennessee’s most closely watched death-penalty cases in decades.
Fox News noted the execution would be the first of a woman in Tennessee in more than two centuries.
BREAKING: The Supreme Court has cleared the way for Tennessee to carry out the execution of death row inmate Christa Pike, lifting a lower court’s stay. She would become the state’s first woman executed in more than 200 years. pic.twitter.com/6id5lXTpDn
— Fox News (@FoxNews) September 30, 2026
Pike was 18 when she took part in the 1995 killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student at a Knoxville job-training center.
Prosecutors said Slemmer was lured away, beaten and stabbed in a prolonged attack. Pike was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death in 1996.
The brutality of Slemmer’s murder should never disappear behind the procedural language of the appeals.
A victim was tortured and killed. Her family then spent more than 30 years watching courts revisit a sentence imposed for that crime.
The Associated Press reported that witnesses had gathered at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville when the Sixth Circuit issued its stay roughly an hour before the scheduled lethal injection.
The appeals court said it needed time to consider Pike’s argument that evidence about severe childhood abuse had not been fully weighed at sentencing. Her attorneys also pointed to her age at the time of the murder and her mental-health history.
Tennessee argued that the litigation had already run for decades and that the victim’s family was entitled to finality. Slemmer’s mother had traveled to Nashville to witness the execution after years of waiting.
The AP said Justice Sotomayor wrote that the Court’s ruling allowed the execution to proceed while legal challenges were still pending. Justices Kagan and Jackson joined her dissent, while the Court’s majority vacated the stay.
Governor Bill Lee had denied Pike’s clemency request on Monday, leaving the courts as her remaining avenue for relief.
The Supreme Court’s decision was the decisive legal development.
The Associated Press announced the reversal after the Sixth Circuit’s intervention.
BREAKING: The Supreme Court allows Tennessee’s execution of Christa Gail Pike to go forward, overturning a last-minute stay. https://t.co/7SxXYFJX4x
— The Associated Press (@AP) September 30, 2026
The Gateway Pundit reported that the Supreme Court acted after Tennessee challenged the last-minute stay and asked the justices to let the execution move forward.
The report emphasized the rapid reversal: Pike had been scheduled for lethal injection Wednesday morning, the Sixth Circuit paused the process, and the Supreme Court later removed that pause.
It also identified the three dissenting justices and placed the ruling against Pike’s conviction for Slemmer’s 1995 murder. That context matters because the emergency litigation concerned whether the sentence could be carried out, not whether Pike committed the crime.
The Court’s action returned the case to the posture Tennessee sought. The state was legally free to proceed, while officials still had to carry out the execution within the remaining life of the warrant.
This was not a new trial and it was not an acquittal fight.
It was a final-hour battle over whether another court-imposed delay would stop a sentence that had survived decades of litigation.
The Sixth Circuit said wait.
The Supreme Court said Tennessee could proceed.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Clears Tennessee Execution of Christa Pike
sources.text:
The Supreme Court cleared the path for Tennessee to execute Christa Pike for a 1995 torture murder, the state's first execution of a woman in 200 years.
The Hill reported that the U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday refused to stop the scheduled lethal injection of Tennessee death-row inmate Christa Pike, convicted in the 1995 killing of teenage classmate Colleen Slemmer.
Pike, now 50 and the lone woman on the state's death row, was set for execution at 10 a.m. local time Wednesday at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Gov. Bill Lee had already refused clemency earlier in the week. The high court gave no explanation for the denial, which landed less than a day before the deadline.
For Slemmer's family, the ruling closed a three-decade wait for final judgment after a crime prosecutors described as a lure, a beating, and a prolonged killing at an abandoned steam plant near the University of Tennessee agricultural campus.
Pike and Slemmer were fellow workers at a Jobs Corps Center. Both were 19. Court documents show Pike claimed Slemmer had been “trying to get [her] boyfriend.” Prosecutors said Pike and that then-boyfriend lured Slemmer to the steam plant, where she was beaten, tortured, and killed.
Pike confessed. She admitted slashing Slemmer's throat several times, throwing asphalt at her head, and keeping a piece of her skull as a souvenir. Authorities also found a pentagram carved into Slemmer's chest. Pike has denied carving it herself.
In 1996 she was convicted of first-degree murder. At 21 she became the youngest person locked on Tennessee's death row. The Tennessee Department of Correction later recorded another first-degree murder conviction tied to an August 2001 assault on fellow inmate Patricia Jones.
May Martinez, Slemmer's mother, told local affiliate WKRN she wanted the sentence carried out. “Maybe now finally we have the justice,” she said. She added: “It may not bring my daughter back, but it might save another person from getting killed because she will do it again.”
Readers who follow last-minute capital litigation have seen similar end-stage fights, including when Alabama moved to execute Jeffery Lee after separate Supreme Court action on method.
Federal public defenders pressed childhood “extreme sexual abuse,” including rape, and said that mitigating history was not fully put before the jury at sentencing. Pike has since been diagnosed with PTSD and bipolar disorder, the reporting states. Her petition called her a “mentally ill 18-year-old kid” at the time of the crime and said she had “changed significantly” in prison.
In her state clemency petition, Pike wrote: “It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done.”
She continued: “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”
Her Supreme Court filing also argued that the lethal-injection protocol, paired with her medical conditions, would cause “extreme psychological torture when extracted from her cell and strapped to the execution gurney,” which she cast as a constitutional violation. The Court was not persuaded.
Death-penalty cases often turn on late process claims long after a jury's verdict, a pattern also visible when Harris County dropped a death-penalty bid in a separate extradition fight.
Breitbart reported that Pike's team sought an all-women lethal-injection crew, citing PTSD tied to abuse by males, or hanging as an alternative, while also pleading for clemency. Attorneys wrote, “Christa was broken, not evil.” The same account set the execution date as September 30 and noted she was the first woman sentenced to death in Tennessee in 200 years.
Martinez rejected the special-treatment ask. “I don't think she should be allowed to have any special treatment,” she told the Daily Mail, adding that Pike “didn't consider how my daughter felt, she's just playing the system... It's all bulls***.”
Gov. Lee's refusal to grant clemency left the Supreme Court as the final backstop. The justices declined to intervene. Parallel emergency appeals at the high court have ended the same way in other high-stakes disputes, including when the Supreme Court rejected surrogate McKenna West's last-ditch bid to block a California custody order.
Pike's case ran from a 1995 killing to a 1996 murder conviction, a second first-degree murder count in 2001, a governor's clemency denial, and a Supreme Court refusal on the eve of the warrant. The method set by the state was lethal injection at Riverbend in Nashville.
Slemmer was 19, from Knoxville. She never came home. Her mother waited through every appeal and every claim of changed character. The courts and the governor kept the sentence intact.
Late stays and emergency filings are familiar terrain in capital cases and in other frantic Supreme Court races against a clock, as when the Supreme Court refused to block a California custody order in a surrogate mother's fight over the child she carried.
Another related high-court endgame came when the Supreme Court let a California custody order stand, closing that dispute after sustained emergency pressure.
Crime has victims who do not get a reprieve. When a jury convicts, a governor denies mercy, and the Supreme Court stands down, the sentence means what it says.

Christa Pike, convicted of murdering a classmate three decades ago, has survived Tennessee’s effort to execute her by means of lethal injection, prison officials said.
Her lawyers said that she had left the prison in an ambulance on Wednesday night and was being treated at a hospital, where she was described as in critical condition.

“Christa is alive right now. We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment,” lawyer Randy Spivey said during a Thursday news conference. “But we know she is alive right now and receiving live-saving medical care.”
Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her lawyers said in court filings.
Journalists who witnessed Wednesday’s attempted execution described snoring, loud exhales, gasps and complaints from Pike about pain, as well as her kicking her feet so often that she knocked off the sheets laid over her, according to NBC News.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee said in a statement that he has ordered “a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred” and that the remaining scheduled execution will not take place this year.
“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” he said.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that they “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office”.
The state’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.
Supreme Court ruling
Pike, 50, had been scheduled to be executed on Wednesday for a murder she committed at age 18. Her killing would have been Tennessee’s first execution of a woman in at least 200 years.
An appeals court ruling stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start, but a Supreme Court ruling later overturned the stay.
Following the top court’s ruling, officials attempted to go ahead with the execution as planned.
At 7:46pm local time (23:46 GMT), prison officials closed the curtain separating Pike from the media viewing room. It was raised three minutes later, when witnesses said Pike could be heard snoring loudly.
The curtain was closed again at 8:06pm. Witnesses continued to hear Pike snoring until the microphone was switched off at about 8:53pm (00:53 GMT), when they were told to leave the area. Emergency vehicles were seen coming and going from the prison.
Earlier, the execution had been halted when the 6th Circuit US Court of Appeals voted 2-1 to issue a stay.
The appeals court said a delay was needed to consider whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered during her sentencing.
Later on Wednesday, the Supreme Court cleared the way for the execution. Its conservative majority did not explain the decision, while the three liberal justices dissented. Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote that vacating the stay “unnecessarily prevents” the appeals court from giving due consideration to Pike’s claim.
Tennessee’s attorney general had argued that delaying the execution traumatised the family of Pike’s victim, Colleen Slemmer, and rewarded what it called “abusive delay tactics”.
The killing in 1995
Pike and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, were convicted of the fatal stabbing and beating in 1995 of 19-year-old Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville.
Shipp was 17 when the crime happened and received a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole. Pike was the only one sentenced to death.
Pike does not deny committing the killing, but her supporters argue the state should consider her age at the time, her mental illness and her allegations of severe sexual abuse, including that she was raped from early childhood.
“It is inconceivable that in the 21st century, the criminal justice system is poised to execute a survivor of rape and child sexual abuse whose jury never had the opportunity to consider those facts in weighing the defendant’s moral culpability,” her lawyers wrote in a filing.
After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and posttraumatic stress disorder.
In her clemency petition, she said she had initially intended to fight Slemmer but killed her in a frenzied attack when she could not “put the brakes on”.
“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realise the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement.
Slemmer’s mother has said she wants Pike’s death sentence carried out after waiting decades for the execution.
Tennessee has not executed a woman for at least 200 years, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Since the Supreme Court reinstated the death penalty in 1976, 18 women have been executed in the US, representing about 1 percent of all executions, according to the centre.

But the Tennessee attorney general's office immediately asked the US Supreme Court to vacate the stay. And the high court's decision siding with Tennessee marked the final word on whether the execution was permitted to go forward before her death warrant expires at midnight CDT (1pm, Singapore time).
The state did not give a precise new time frame for the execution, which was set to take place at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, the state capital.
If the state were to run out of time to conduct the execution, it would need to obtain a new warrant from the Tennessee Supreme Court, according to Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center.

Pike was 18 in January 1995 when she, a 17-year-old boyfriend and a third companion lured 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate at their Knoxville Job Corps vocational centre, into a wooded area where they tortured and killed her.
The grisly nature of the slaying, which involved the perpetrators carving the shape of a pentagram in the victim's chest and taking a chunk of her skull as a souvenir of the carnage, drew intense media coverage at the time.
Trial testimony indicated that Pike viewed Slemmer as a rival for the affections of her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp.
Pike and Shipp were both convicted of first-degree murder. Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Their co-defendant, Shadolla Peterson, who was 18 at the time of the murder and acted as a lookout for the other two, testified for the prosecution and received probation.
Currently the only woman on Tennessee's death row, Pike was also convicted in August 2001 of attempted first-degree murder in an assault on another inmate, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction.
TEEN WHO COMMITTED MURDER "NO LONGER EXISTS"
In the 226-page petition asking the governor to commute her death penalty to a life sentence without the possibility of parole, Pike's lawyers documented her history as the childhood victim of violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including two rapes at ages 11 and 17. They also cited the diagnoses she received in prison for bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Moreover, they pointed to evidence that Pike's mother drank heavily during pregnancy, contributing to faulty brain development that made it difficult for their client to control her impulses as a young person.
"The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists," her lawyers wrote in response to Lee's denial of clemency.
"Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women."
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, has spoken out in support of the execution.
Executions of female prison inmates are exceedingly rare in the US, with women accounting for just 18 of the 1,683 people put to death since the Supreme Court allowed capital punishment to resume in 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Before Wednesday, Tennessee had executed 17 people.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday night cleared the way for the execution of Christa Pike, the only woman on Tennessee’s death row. Justice Sonia Sotomayor dissented from the decision to lift the stay of execution, in a three-page opinion that was joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson. Sotomayor wrote that she saw “no reason to short-circuit the ordinary process of appellate review, particularly in light of the grave consequences of an erroneous decision.”
Pike was convicted and sentenced to death for the brutal 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer. She sought post-conviction relief in state court, arguing that at her sentencing her trial counsel should have presented evidence regarding the sexual abuse that she suffered as a child. Her efforts to obtain state and federal post-conviction relief were unsuccessful.
On Tuesday, Pike filed a motion in federal court to reopen her federal post-conviction case. She pointed to the state’s recent concession – at odds, she said, with its prior contentions – that she “was a teenaged survivor of child sexual abuse and rape who was struggling with unmedicated bipolar disorder and PTSD at the time of her crime.”
By a vote of 2-1, the 6th Circuit on Wednesday morning put Pike’s execution on hold to give that court time to consider the arguments made by Pike and the state.
The state came quickly to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to lift the lower court’s order. It called Pike’s latest filing an “abusive, tactical delay” and “nothing more than an attempt to relitigate the merits of” a claim that had already been rejected.
Pike countered that, even if the lower courts ultimately do not grant her motion to reopen the federal case, “[a]t the very least,” the Supreme Court “should allow the Sixth Circuit to issue its decision.” “It is inconceivable,” she said, “that in the 21st century, the criminal justice system is poised to execute a survivor of rape and child sexual abuse whose jury never had the opportunity to consider those facts in weighing the defendant’s moral culpability.”

A spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Correction told the Associated Press that “it would proceed with Pike’s execution Wednesday night ahead of a midnight cutoff on the state’s execution order.”

A condemned female murderer who survived two attempted lethal injections during a botched execution by the US state of Tennessee was in critical condition and receiving "life-saving care", her lawyer said.
Tennessee officials were unable to put Christa Pike to death yesterday for a 1995 murder despite administering two doses of a lethal drug.
"Christa is alive right now," said Randall Spivey, who is one of Pike's lawyers.
"What we have been told is that she is in critical condition, receiving life-saving care," Mr Spivey said in a virtual news conference.
He urged Governor Bill Lee, who had denied a clemency request earlier in the week, to scrap Pike's death sentence.
"After having endured solitary confinement for more than 20 years and a full attempt to kill her by lethal injection, Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty. The governor must commute Christa's sentence now."
Pike was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and taken by ambulance from the prison, her lawyers said earlier.
Pike, 50, had been scheduled for execution at 10am local time yesterday for the killing she committed at the age of 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start and hours later, the US Supreme Court overturned that stay.
Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her lawyers said in court filings late yesterday.
Her lawyers repeated their calls for Pike's sentence to be commuted to life in prison after enduring what they called "chemical torture."
A death penalty expert said it was an unprecedented failure.
Robin M Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Centre, said what Pike experienced is "singular and unparalleled".
'Nothing about today was normal,' say media witnesses
She appears to be the first person known to have survived after execution drugs entered her body, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a non-profit group in Washington.
Seven other people have survived medical problems due to the execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.
Pike's lawyers said: "We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: Difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy."
Media witnesses observing from a separate room said officials raised curtains to the execution chamber at 7.27pm, showing Pike strapped to a gurney.
Pike remained awake and at one point raised her head and asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way. It was not clear what she was referencing.
By 8.26pm, execution witnesses reported that the second dose of pentobarbital had been administered.
Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8.53pm.
At that time there was an announcement to escort media witnesses out of the area.
Tennessee Department of Correction spokesperson Dorinda Carter told media witnesses she was unable to immediately provide information about what happened.
Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late yesterday to the US Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in "unnecessary agony" and it was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.
They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit court and District Court.
The motion also asserted that the Department of Correction should begin lifesaving measures: "Failure to provide such care constitutes deliberate indifference to legitimate, serious medical needs."
Ex-prosecutor says failed execution raises 'practical concerns'
Former US federal prosecutor Joe Moreno said what happens next to Pike is up to the Governor of Tennessee.
Speaking on RTÉ's Six One, he said the drug pentobarbital is supposed to be the most effective and efficient narcotic used in executing a prisoner, causing the least amount of suffering.
But now that it did not work on Ms Pike, it raises "practical concerns".
Mr Moreno said the failed execution might now incentivise the US to revisit the moral and legal basis by which it enforces capital punishment.
However, he said the majority of Americans still support the death penalty according to opinion polls and want to see it continue. He said he does not see it going away.
He said that the thinking behind the injection is a combination of what is supposed to be the most humane to the person being executed as far as reducing his or her suffering but also reducing the graphic nature of seeing someone being electrocuted or being asphyxiated in a gas chamber or being shot by a firing squad.
On what happens next to Pike, he said a pause or a continuation of the sentence is a "possibility", however, he said there have also been arguments to engage a firing squad.
He said the firing squad is the most effective means of doing this, but it has not been used for a long time.
Pike, boyfriend convicted of stabbing classmate in 1995
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of the fatal stabbing and beating in 1995 of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville.
The case garnered widespread attention in part because a pentagram that was carved on Ms Slemmer's body and other elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the "satanic panic" of the 1980s and 1990s.
It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to carry out an execution.
In May, state officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried and failed for over an hour to place an IV to administer pentobarbital.
Pike was initially scheduled to be put to death in the morning, and witnesses had gathered at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville when the Sixth Circuit US Court of Appeals voted 2-1 to issue a stay.
Pike's lawyers had argued she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of the killing.
They said her history of childhood sexual assault, post traumatic stress disorder and a blood condition meant a lethal injection would cause "needless suffering".
That court said a delay was needed to consider whether Pike's allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her sentencing.
The attorney general's office appealed to the Supreme Court, saying that halting the execution at the last moment traumatised Ms Slemmer's family and rewarded "abusive delay tactics" by Pike's attorneys.
Later in the day, the High Court cleared the way for the execution to proceed.
The conservative majority did not explain their order, while the three liberal members signed a dissent that said Pike's claims deserved a closer look.
Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote in the dissent that the decision to vacate the stay interfered with the Sixth Circuit court's handling of the case and "unnecessarily prevents that court from giving due consideration to Pike's claim".
Tennessee will halt an execution planned for later this year, said Governor Bill Lee, according to US media.
"The remaining scheduled execution will not be carried out this year," Mr Lee was quoted as saying in a statement carried by the Tennessean and NewsNation, adding he was calling for a "comprehensive, third-party review" of the failed execution of Pike.

US death row inmate survives execution attempt after two lethal injections

Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has been taken to hospital after an attempt to execute her by two lethal injections failed, her lawyer says.
Her legal team filed an emergency motion to halt the convicted murderer's execution as it was happening, saying: "Ms Pike has lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring."
One of her attorneys told the BBC that the 50-year-old was now "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital after two syringes of pentobarbital had been administered.
Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Her execution was the subject of a last-minute legal battle.
This culminated in the US Supreme Court allowing the lethal injections to go ahead.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
Slemmer's mother May Martinez was among those who wanted the execution to take place. She told NBC News after Wednesday evening's events: "It was a mess."
The attempted execution took place at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville at about 20:00 local time (01:00 GMT on Thursday).
Pike was given two doses of the chemical pentobarbital and the curtain in the witness room was closed twice, the Associated Press reported.
Media were at some point asked to leave, the news agency said.
AP added that Tennessee's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of pentobarbital-filled syringes in case the person being put to death does not die after the first set. But it does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee said in a statement reported by US media that he had ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred". He said the year's last remaining execution would not go ahead as planned.
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in the state in 2026 that did not unfold as planned. The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has said it stood by all the actions it took during the attempted execution of Pike.
Department spokeswoman Dorinda Carter told the Tennessean newspaper that it had "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General's Office".
She said: "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility."
Pike's legal team said in a statement to the Tennessean newspaper: "Tonight the state of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution.
"We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy."
Pike's lawyers filed an emergency motion to stay her execution and provide medical care after the lethal injection was apparently botched.
District Judge Clifton L Corker issued a ruling noting that "medical personnel have begun to administer medical care as requested in the motion".
Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine who told the BBC he had been retained by Pike's legal team as a medical expert, said she likely never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause apnoea and cardiovascular failure during the attempted execution.
"It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury," Zivot said.
The attempted capital punishment went ahead after multiple last-minute legal challenges by Pike's lawyers failed.
The US Supreme Court had thwarted two separate efforts to stop the lethal injection.
Late on Wednesday, the highest US court overturned a reprieve granted by a lower court earlier in the day. The lower court had granted a pause, saying it needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case.
The Supreme Court had previously dismissed an appeal by Pike's lawyers, who had argued the jury did not get the chance to weigh mitigating evidence of Pike's documented history of childhood sexual abuse before they sentenced her to death in 1996.
The defence said that for years, the state of Tennessee had argued in court that she lied about being sexually abused as a child.
But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the state said it did not dispute that she had suffered sexual abuse and rape.
Tennessee's governor denied a clemency request this week from Pike, the only woman on the state's death row.
Pike said in her clemency petition that she intended to beat Slemmer, not kill her, but that she was unable to "put the brakes on".
"I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid," she said. "It took me numerous years to even realise the gravity of what I'd done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."
The murder in 1995 created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee, after Colleen was found with an inverted pentagram - a symbol that is associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest. Pike has denied carving the symbol herself.
Before the killing, Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her then-boyfriend.
Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.
Pike's boyfriend and co-defendant Shipp was 17 at the time so was spared the death penalty under state law. He remains in prison.
Martinez, Slemmer's mother, said at the weekend that she had waited decades to see Pike's sentence carried out.
She told AP that a group helped raise funds for her and her husband to travel from Florida to Tennessee to witness the execution.
"Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst," Martinez said.
Since 1976, when the Supreme Court resumed the death penalty, only 18 women have been executed in the US, compared to 1,663 men. That is about 1% of all US executions.

sources.text:
A divided U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday cleared the way for Tennessee to move forward with the execution of Christa Pike, lifting a last-minute stay issued by a federal appeals court less than two hours before she was scheduled to die by lethal injection.
In a 6-3 decision, the high court granted Tennessee’s emergency request to lift the temporary block. Pike, who tortured and murdered a classmate, is set to become the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
The ruling allows Tennessee to carry out the execution before Pike’s death warrant expires at midnight local time Wednesday.
Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
“Because its decision clears the way for the State to execute Pike before her still-pending legal challenges to her conviction can be properly considered, I respectfully dissent,” Sotomayor wrote for the liberal wing.
Hours before the Supreme Court’s intervention, a divided 2-1 panel of the 6th Circuit blocked the execution to consider claims that Pike’s jury never heard about her childhood sexual abuse. Judge Richard Griffin dissented, calling the bid a “last-ditch meritless effort to delay a lawful execution,” The Daily Wire reported.
Pike, who is now 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer, 19, a fellow student at the Knoxville Job Corps Center. Pike lured Slemmer into the woods with her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp. Pike cut Slemmer’s throat, struck her with a meat cleaver and with a piece of asphalt before they carved a pentagram into her forehead and chest, according to court documents. Pike kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull as a trophy and bragged about the killing to friends.
In 1996, a jury convicted the then- 18-year-old of first-degree murder. She has spent decades behind bars on death row ever since. In prison, Pike almost strangled fellow inmate Patricia Jones with a shoelace in 2001, landing her a separate attempted first-degree murder conviction.
Pike’s attorneys argued that she suffered lasting trauma from childhood sexual abuse that her trial lawyers failed to adequately present to the jury. Court records say the abuse began when Pike was 2. She was later raped by a stranger living nearby and by her mother’s live-in boyfriend, The Daily Wire reported.
Her attorneys asked Tennessee Republican Gov. Bill Lee to intervene, but he declined. “After deliberate consideration of Christa Gail Pike’s request for clemency, and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding the sentence of the State of Tennessee and do not plan to intervene,” Lee said Monday.
Her attorneys said they were “deeply saddened and heartbroken” by his decision. And in a dramatic reversal, Pike says she now feels remorse. “I’m very remorseful now; I wasn’t in the beginning when I first caught this charge,” she said. “I didn’t care what I had done.”
“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike added in her clemency petition.

Who Was Colleen Slemmer And What Was Her Family Like?
Born on 20 September 1975, Slemmer grew up in Orange Park, Florida, with her mother, May Martinez, stepfather Raul Martinez, and younger sister.
Family members have described her as compassionate, easygoing, and someone who regularly helped others.
Martinez recalled that Slemmer volunteered with the Special Olympics, helped children with disabilities, and enjoyed roller skating. She struggled with reading, but her mother described her as intelligent, with a strong interest in computers that eventually shaped her future plans.
Slemmer enrolled at the Knoxville Job Corps Center because it offered computer training that was not available at the programme near her Florida home. In late 1994, she left her family to pursue the vocational course, where she became a classmate of Pike and other students involved in the case.
How Christa Pike and Her Accomplices Attacked Colleen
On 11 January 11 1995, Pike told fellow Job Corps student Kim Iloilo that she intended to kill Slemmer because she 'had just felt mean that day'. The following evening, Pike, her boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, and Shadolla Peterson left the centre with Slemmer and headed towards an area near the University of Tennessee.

A jury convicted Pike in 1996 of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit first-degree murder. The jury imposed the death penalty after finding that the murder involved torture or serious physical abuse beyond that necessary to cause death.
Shipp, who was 17 at the time of the killing, received a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Peterson, who acted as a lookout and later testified for the prosecution, received probation.

Pike, now 50, was convicted in the brutal 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate at the Knoxville Job Corps. Prosecutors said Pike, afraid Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend, lured her to a wooded area on Jan. 12, 1995.
Pike tortured Slemmer to death and caved in her head with a large rock.
A pentagram was carved into Slemmer’s chest, and investigators said Pike saved a piece of her victim’s skull as a souvenir to the murder. Pike’s boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, has admitted he carved the pentagram. Shipp was 17 and received life in prison with the possibility of parole. Pike was the only one sentenced to death.
Pike was also convicted in a 2001 attack on fellow inmate Patricia Jones.
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, traveled from Florida to witness the execution. She said she thinks about her daughter constantly and that her daughter would have turned 51 this month.
“Holidays are the worst,” Martinez said.
Earlier this week, she said she hoped she would finally see justice.
Pike does not deny the murder.
Her attorneys argue she should be spared because she was 18 at the time, was mentally ill and had been sexually abused since she was a toddler. They also argued that being strapped down by male executioners would cause her extreme psychological torture because of her past rapes. A special master appointed by the Tennessee Supreme Court rejected that claim, finding that mental suffering alone does not violate the Constitution’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment.
If the execution goes forward, Pike will be the first woman executed in Tennessee in at least 200 years. She would be only the 19th woman put to death in the U.S. since 1976, when capital punishment resumed.

Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike receiving medical care after failed execution
Media witnesses describe a scene of confusion; Pike receiving medical care after the second round of Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol
Emergency vehicles at Riverbend Maximum Security Prison in Nashville on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. The execution of death row inmate Christa Pike was halted nearly two hours after the state of Tennessee began the lethal injection protocol. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
The Wednesday execution of Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike was halted after the state of Tennessee administered two failed rounds of its lethal injection protocol and federal public defenders filed an emergency appeal to end the execution and get Pike medical care.
The botched execution spanned more than two hours, according to media witnesses. Pike was still making audible “snoring” sounds when witnesses were told to exit the building about 40 minutes after the curtains to the execution chamber closed for the second time.
Pike was taken by ambulance to a hospital for treatment, according to a spokesperson for the U.S. Campaign to End the Death Penalty, but the group did not know her medical status. Witnesses reported seeing ambulances pulling up to Riverbend Maximum Security Prison in Nashville, the site of the execution, and leaving with lights on.
Media witnesses described a scene of confusion.
“Very obviously, we have a lot of questions about what we saw and what we did not see, because there were moments when the blinds were down for us, and there were moments when the blinds were up for us,” said John North, investigative producer for WBIR TV in Knoxville. “It appeared that this did not go like they thought it was supposed to go, but we don’t know that.”
“When we left the building, so far as we knew, she was probably still alive,” North said. “You just saw the emergency vehicles pull up. We don’t know her status, and I think it’s fair to say … we have a lot of questions, and the Department of Correction has a lot of answers that it needs to provide to the public about what happened here.”
“The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office,” department Communications Director Dorinda Carter stated more than two hours after the failed execution. “The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility.”
Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol stipulates that a second round of injections be performed if the inmate is not determined to be deceased after the first set is administered. It does not specify what happens if the second set also fails.
Federal defense attorneys for Pike filed an emergency motion with the U.S. District Court of the Eastern District of Tennessee to halt the execution and order immediate medical care.
Pike’s attorneys also filed a motion to halt the execution in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit at 10:20 p.m.
“Since the botched execution in May of this year, people from diverse political backgrounds across Tennessee have called for a pause in executions to examine the problems with the execution process. These pleas were ignored. The state of Tennessee has shown the world it cannot be trusted to implement capital punishment in a way that preserves human dignity and the rule of law. This has to stop now,” said Laura Porter, the anti-death penalty group’s executive director.
The U.S. Supreme Court vacated the temporary stay of Christa Pike’s execution Wednesday evening, allowing the state of Tennessee to move forward with her death by lethal injection for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer.
“I’ve witnessed, I believe, five executions in Tennessee,” said Tori Gessner with WKRN News 2 in Nashville. “Nothing about today was normal, typical at all, and the court delay was just the tip of the iceberg.”
Pike was set to be executed at 10 a.m. Wednesday before a federal appeals court temporarily halted the execution to review Pike’s history of sexual abuse and neglect as a child, which Pike’s lawyers say was not adequately addressed during the penalty phase in her original trial.
Pike, 50, was set to be the first female put to death in Tennessee in nearly two centuries.
Pike was 18 years old when she and her then-17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in a wooded area in Knoxville. Shipp, ineligible for the death penalty because of his age, got a life sentence.
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, described her daughter as compassionate, playful and a “good nerd” in a recent interview with WBIR Knoxville.
Witnesses say curtain remained closed for most of two-hour process
Witnesses entered the witness chamber at 6:41 p.m. and waited for nearly an hour, something media witnesses who have covered prior executions in Tennessee said was atypical. During that time, they described hearing groaning and crying, though the microphone inside the execution chamber was not yet turned on and the curtain remained closed.
The curtain opened for the first time at 7:26 p.m.
In Pike’s final statement, she said she was “going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life, and that is in love,” Kim Chandler of AP reported. “She said she had love for the people who were out here hating on her.”
“She closed her statement with saying, ‘I’m at peace. I’m ready to be free,’ then something about celebrating her freedom, and then she closed with, ‘This is a happy day,’” Chandler said.
Pike said “My arm feels like it’s about to burst open” at 7:34 p.m., Gessner said.
Will Puckett of WVLT Knoxville described Pike blinking, smiling and letting out “a couple of laughs during this process.”
“I saw a tear roll down (from) her right eye, and then she said, ‘one spot is really throbbing,’” Puckett said.
Pike began to speak less and take big breaths, and lifted her head up at 7:39 p.m. Throughout the process, Pike “was kicking her feet so often that she was actually knocking the sheet that laid over her off,” Puckett said.
An employee placed a rock in view of witnesses for the first time at 7:41 p.m. and 30 seconds. Media witnesses at other executions said this is part of the state’s process, and while it’s unclear exactly what the rock signifies, it’s typical for subjects to appear “comatose” by the time the rock is placed. But Pike’s jaws were moving, and she said something three minutes later, then opened her mouth wide “like a very large yawn.”
The curtain dropped for the first time at 7:46 p.m., before opening back up three minutes later. Pike began to sound as if she were loudly snoring, media witnesses said. Her spiritual adviser was brought back into the room.
Puckett described Pike’s lip quivering and Pike making sounds “like she was almost choking.” Pike continued making snoring sounds and at 7:54 p.m. she grunted, lifted her head and opened her mouth, Puckett said.
Two minutes later, “her body lifted off the gurney again, both her head and her legs” in a “v” shape, Puckett said.
The rock was placed for a second time at 8:01 p.m. and six seconds. Media witnesses reported Pike continued breathing and making snoring sounds, flexing her head and neck.
The curtain closed for the final time at 8:05 p.m., and media witnesses said Pike snored in a consistent, rhythmic pattern interspersed with the sounds of doors opening and closing until 8:53 p.m., when witnesses were escorted out.
“I cannot emphasize enough how much of whatever just happened, happened behind a closed curtain,” Steven Hale of the Nashville Banner said. “When Christa Pike was still alive, we could still hear her breathing, but we could not see what was going on.”
Hours of uncertainty pending court decisions preceded execution attempt
Before Wednesday’s last-minute pause, the nation’s highest court and Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, had declined to intervene to stop Pike’s execution.
The three-judge panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit stayed Pike’s execution Wednesday morning because more time was needed to “adequately address and resolve the issues” brought by Pike’s lawyers, the ruling stated.
The U.S. Supreme Court affirmed the state’s request to proceed with the execution late Wednesday in response to the Tennessee attorney general’s appeal of the 6th Circuit panel’s temporary stay. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
“The Court’s decision to vacate that stay interferes with the Sixth Circuit’s routine administrative handling of a capital case and unnecessarily prevents that court from giving due consideration to Pike’s claim,” Sotomayor wrote in the dissenting opinion. “Worse, the Court grants such extraordinary relief solely to allow the state to execute Pike before litigation over her conviction has properly run its course in the lower courts.”
“I see no reason to short-circuit the ordinary process of appellate review, particularly in light of the grave consequences of an erroneous decision,” Sotomayor continued. “Tennessee’s desire to expedite Pike’s execution by a few days or even weeks cannot outweigh her ‘fundamental interest in (her) own life.’”
Pike’s execution is the latest to be botched by the Tennessee Department of Correction.
In May, Gov. Bill Lee called off the execution of Tony Von Carruthers after a physician tried for more than an hour to insert backup and central intravenous lines on Carruthers, as required by protocol. Witnesses called it bloody “torture.”
This is a developing story and may be updated.
Sam Stockard, Adam Friedman and J. Holly McCall contributed to this report.

More than three decades after 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer was killed in Tennessee, her mother continues to remember the young woman she was before her name got linked to a notorious murder case.

As Christa Pike's scheduled execution approaches in Tennessee, attention has once again turned to the 19-year-old whose murder put Pike on death row more than three decades ago.
Colleen Slemmer was a young woman from Orange Park, Florida, who left home in 1994 to pursue career training at the Knoxville Job Corps. She was studying computing, and her family had hopes for a bright future when she was brutally killed. Christa Pike, who was 18 at the time, was convicted of Slemmer's murder and sentenced to death.
Who was Christa Pike's victim, Colleen Slemmer?
Born on September 20, 1975, Colleen Slemmer grew up in Florida in a family that remembers her as caring, independent, and eager to help others. Her mother, May Martinez, ran a daycare for decades, and she has said Colleen naturally developed a love for children.
Slemmer babysat and volunteered with the Special Olympics, where she spent time helping children with special needs. She also had a strong interest in computers, and that passion eventually led her to the Job Corps, where she met Christa Pike. Colleen's family revealed that she left her Florida home for Knoxville in October 1994. She was enrolled at the Knoxville Job Corps with Pike and Pike's then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp.
On January 12, 1995, Slemmer was found in a gnarly state in a secluded, wooded area of the University of Tennessee campus. She had more than 300 slashes and lacerations across her body, with a pentagram deeply carved into her chest. Prosecutors said Pike viewed Slemmer as a romantic rival who wanted to steal Tadaryl from her.
Slemmer lay lifeless behind a steam plant on the university campus, near Tyson Park in Knoxville. Her skull was severely crushed by a huge asphalt rock that Pike had hit her with. She even took out the broken portion of Slemmer's skull, physically carved it, and later showed it off as a souvenir to other students at the Job Corps.
What happened to Christa Pike's accomplices?
Pike has never denied her role in Slemmer's killing. In a statement included in her clemency petition, she expressed remorse and acknowledged the lasting impact of what she did. Pike wrote:
"I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."
Pike was the only one of the three to receive a death sentence. Her accomplice, Tadaryl Shipp, 17, was a minor at the time of the murder, so Tennessee law didn't grant him a death penalty. He is now serving a life sentence in a Tennessee state prison after his first parole was denied recently.
The third participant, Shadolla Peterson, never served prison time and is out of custody because she acted as the lookout during the murder and turned state's evidence. She cooperated fully with the prosecutors and testified against both Pike and Shipp.
Pike's attorneys have argued in recent years that significant information about her severe childhood abuse, neglect, and mental health conditions was not adequately presented during the sentencing phase of her trial. However, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee rejected Pike's clemency request on September 28, 2026, saying he would uphold the state's sentence.
The U.S. Supreme Court also rejected a last-minute request to halt the execution, according to current reporting. For Slemmer's mother, however, the years of legal arguments surrounding Pike do not change what was lost in 1995.
Who are Colleen Slemmer's parents?
Slemmer's biological father was Michael Deacy, who attended Christa Pike's 1996 trial. Since then, he has largely stayed out of the public eye. Her mother, May, has spent more than 30 years keeping her daughter's memory alive. She later married Raul Martinez, who has been a constant presence by May's side through the decades since the tragedy.
Now, as Pike's execution date arrives, Colleen's family is preparing to return to Tennessee once again. This time, May and Raul Martinez plan to be there as the state carries out the sentence imposed for the death of the young woman they never stopped mourning.
Days before Pike's scheduled execution, Colleen's mother made a big statement to the public. Speaking to WKRN, May Martinez said:
"Maybe now finally we have the justice...It may not bring my daughter back, but it might save another person from getting killed because she will do it again."
Pike's execution will be conducted on September 30, 2026, at 10 a.m. CDT, at Nashville's Riverbend Maximum Security Institution. It will be strictly private, with only authorized witnesses allowed inside the execution chamber.
Days before her execution, Christa Pike said that she is now "at peace" and "not afraid to die." She has also refused to have her final meal before the lethal injection.
For Colleen's family, Christa Pike's execution marks the end of a decades-long legal journey and a closure to the painful loss of their daughter.

Sole female death row inmate set for execution; A look back on Christa Pike’s case and a letter she wrote days before her execution
Pike was convicted in the torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville back in 1995
What This Story Is About
- Christa Pike is set to become the first woman executed by the state of Tennessee in more than 200 years, and the first in the modern death penalty era, for the 1995 killing of her Job Corps colleague Colleen Slemmer.
Why It Matters
- The case has drawn national attention because Tennessee’s death penalty law now requires an “enhanced killing” rather than a killing alone, making Pike’s case legally distinct from earlier executions of women in the state.
What Happens Next
- Barring any last-minute changes, Pike is set to be executed at 10 a.m. Wednesday at Riverbend Prison under conditions including an all-female transport staff and extra privacy, after Governor Bill Lee said he will not intervene.
For Context
- Retired professor Lewis Laska said the only other women executed in Tennessee were enslaved people convicted of killing their own children and the first white woman executed, who killed her husband, while noting women are executed less often due to more sympathetic case circumstances and a modern legal standard requiring aggravating factors.
Catch Up
- Pike, then 18, was convicted of luring, torturing and killing Slemmer, including cutting a pentagram into her body and later throwing a chunk of asphalt at her head, and kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull as a souvenir before she was caught.
- Gov. Lee not intervening in Christa Pike’s execution, only woman on Tennessee’s death row
- Advocates urge Gov. Lee to stop execution of the only woman on Tennessee’s death row
- Christa Pike isn’t Tennessee’s first woman on death row. Here’s who was first
- In letter, Christa Gail Pike says ‘I am not afraid to die’ ahead of Tennessee execution
- Christa Gail Pike, only woman on Tennessee’s death row, declines to pick last meal
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - Christa Pike is set to be the first woman executed by the state of Tennessee in more than 200 years, drawing national attention to her case.
Pike, then 18 years old, killed her Job Corps colleague Colleen Slemmer in 1995. Prosecutors say Pike and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, tortured Slemmer, including cutting a pentagram into her body, before Pike threw a chunk of asphalt at Slemmer’s head, killing her. Prosecutors say the motive was that Pike believed Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend.
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has waited decades for Pike’s sentence to be carried out. She told a sister station in Knoxville about her daughter’s love of computers, roller skating and running marathons.
“Colleen loved doing things. She babysat. She loved to do anything with kids and I think it was part of me because I had daycare for 40 years,” Martinez said.
“See justice for Christa Pike to be put to death to stop, to finally stop this. So no other parent has to feel this pain and hurt,” Martinez said.
Historic case
Pike is not the first woman ever executed by Tennessee, but she would be the first in the modern death penalty era.
Retired attorney and professor Lewis Laska has studied the death penalty in Tennessee for years. He said the other women executed in Tennessee’s history were enslaved people convicted of killing their own children, or women accused of killing their own spouse.
Laska said Pike’s case cannot be directly compared to those older cases because the law has changed.
“You can’t get the death penalty in Tennessee anymore for merely killing your husband or wife. That’s not the law. It has to be an enhanced killing,” Laska said.
The jury found Pike’s crime met that standard. They heard how she lured and killed Slemmer, and how Pike kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull as a souvenir, showing it off to classmates before police caught her.
“That’s pretty drastic, and it’s hard to get past that kind of action,” Laska said. “Again, the facts of the case are everything.”
Why fewer women face execution
Laska said women defendants are often seen as more sympathetic due to the circumstances of their cases. As an example, he cited a woman who was repeatedly sexually abused by her husband and shot him in the back; she was given the death penalty, but the governor commuted her sentence.
Statistics show women are less likely to commit violent crimes that meet the standard for the death penalty. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, women account for only about 1% of all executions in the modern U.S. death penalty era.
Laska said cultural and religious attitudes toward mercy for women also play a role, alongside a modern legal standard requiring a death sentence to involve “enhanced” or aggravated circumstances, rather than a killing alone.
Letter from Pike
A letter from Christa Pike, written days ago, says she is at peace. She writes she is not scared to die, but scared of how it will happen.
Pike’s attorneys argue her past sexual trauma and mental illness should be reasons to call off the execution.
Governor Bill Lee says he will not intervene.
The state has agreed to several conditions intended to make the process easier for Pike, including an all-female staff to transport her to Riverbend Prison and extra privacy when she changes and showers.
Barring any last-minute changes, Christa Pike is set to be executed at 10 a.m. Wednesday.
Pike not the only woman on death row
Pike is not the only female prisoner to have been on death row. She was previously joined by Gaile Owens, a Memphis native who was convicted of hiring a man to kill her then-husband.
Owens’ sentence was commuted by Governor Bredesen, and she was eventually paroled before dying in 2019.

Tennessee is poised to carry out its first execution of a woman in 200 years after the US Supreme Court cleared the way for Christa Pike to be put to death by lethal injection for the killing of a fellow student three decades ago.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that it planned “to move forward with the execution today”.
A defense attorney for Pike said that the execution could be imminent.
“It should start any minute if it hasn’t already,” Luke Ihnen said after the Supreme Court lifted a lower court block of the execution.
Pike, whose clemency petition highlighting childhood trauma and sexual abuse was denied by Governor Bill Lee on Monday, would be the only person in the modern era of US capital punishment to be executed in Tennessee for a crime committed as a teenager.
In an order decided by its 6-3 conservative majority, and signed by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, the Supreme Court lifted a temporary stay of execution that had been granted by a three-judge panel of the 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals one hour before Pike had been scheduled to be put to death.
The appellate panel voted 2-1 to order a “short stay” to allow time to weigh Pike’s claim that evidence of her childhood sexual abuse were not adequately considered during her sentencing.
The US Supreme Court
Pike’s lawyers argued that the sentencing should be reopened because the state’s attorneys had conceded in court for the first time, at a hearing in August, that Pike had suffered from sexual abuse, including rape, as a child.
But the Tennessee attorney general’s office immediately asked the US Supreme Court to vacate the stay. And the high court’s decision siding with Tennessee marked the final word on whether the execution was permitted to go forward, so long as it takes place before her death warrant expires at midnight local time.
The state Department of Correction did not specify a precise new time frame for the execution, which was set to take place at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, the state capital.
If the state were to run out of time to conduct the execution, it would need to obtain a new warrant from the Tennessee Supreme Court, according to Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center.
Pike, now 50, was 18 in January 1995 when she, 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, and a third companion lured 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate at their Knoxville Job Corps vocational centre, into a wooded area where they tortured and killed her.
The grisly nature of the slaying drew intense media coverage at the time.
Trial testimony indicated that Pike viewed Ms Slemmer as a rival for the affections of Shipp.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh signed the order lifting the temporary stay of execution
Pike and Shipp confessed to the killing, and both were convicted the following year of first-degree murder. Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Their co-defendant, Shadolla Peterson, who was 18 at the time of the murder and had acted as a lookout for the other two, appeared as a witness for the prosecution and received probation.
Currently the only woman on Tennessee’s death row, Pike was also convicted in August 2001 of attempted first-degree murder in an assault on another inmate, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction.
In a 226-page petition asking the governor to commute her death penalty to a life sentence without the possibility of parole, her lawyers documented her history as the childhood victim of violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including two rapes at ages 11 and 17.
They cited the diagnoses she received in prison for bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Teen who committed murder ‘no longer exists’
Pike’s lawyers also pointed to evidence that her mother drank heavily during pregnancy, contributing to faulty brain development that made it difficult for their client to control her impulses as a young person.
“The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists,” her lawyers wrote in response to Mr Lee’s denial of clemency.
“Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women.”
Ms Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has spoken out in support of the execution.
Executions of female prison inmates are exceedingly rare in the US, with women accounting for just 18 of the 1,683 people put to death since the Supreme Court allowed capital punishment to resume in 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Pike’s case has drawn international attention, with a group of United Nations human rights experts issuing a recent statement calling for commutation of her death sentence.
Sexual violence and trauma experts have also spoken out on her behalf, arguing that the procedures surrounding lethal injection would likely cause Pike to experience severe, traumatic flashbacks of child sexual abuse and rape, adding to the cruelty and anguish of her death.

The Christa Pike execution is back on after the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday lifted a last minute pause that a federal appeals court had placed on it, clearing Tennessee to put to death the only woman on its death row.
Pike, 50, was scheduled to die by lethal injection at 10 a.m. local time at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. At 8:17 a.m., less than two hours before that time, a three judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit issued what it called a “short stay of execution,” a temporary pause that stops the state from going forward. The panel said it needed time to properly analyze both sides’ arguments and decide the issues on their merits. Judges Karen Moore and Jane Stranch voted for the pause, and Judge Richard Griffin disagreed.
Tennessee went straight to the Supreme Court and asked the justices to throw out the pause. In its filing, the state accused Pike of “abusive, tactical delay” and pointed out that she had not even asked the 6th Circuit for a stay. The Supreme Court granted Tennessee’s request later Wednesday. The order did not overturn Pike’s conviction or her death sentence, and as of publication, it had not been confirmed whether the Christa Pike execution has been carried out or when it will be rescheduled.
The ruling came one day after the Supreme Court turned down a separate request from Pike to stop her execution. That challenge targeted Tennessee’s lethal injection method and the way the state handles lawsuits over it. The justices denied it Tuesday without explanation and with no noted dissents. On Monday, Governor Bill Lee refused to grant clemency, the power a governor has to reduce a sentence or spare someone’s life, saying he did “not plan to intervene.
Pike was 18 when she killed 19 year old Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville in 1995. Both were students at the Knoxville Job Corps, a federal training program for low income young people. Her attorneys have spent years arguing that she should not be executed because of her age at the time of the crime, the physical and sexual abuse she suffered as a child, and later diagnoses of bipolar disorder and post traumatic stress disorder. Pike spent close to three decades in what her lawyers called de facto solitary confinement before a 2024 settlement allowed her to work and share meals with a small group of other women.
If the Christa Pike execution goes forward, she will be the first woman executed in Tennessee since 1820 and only the fourth in the state’s history.

sources.text:
The financial burden of a death sentence ultimately falls on taxpayers, who fund the extensive appeals process prosecutors must pursue in capital cases.
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. — A federal appeals court halted Christa Pike’s execution Wednesday, intervening roughly an hour before she was scheduled to be put to death.
Pike, 50, was due to receive a lethal injection in Tennessee for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer.
Yet the expense of seeking Pike’s execution could match or exceed the cost of keeping her imprisoned for life—an outcome that raises broader questions about the price of capital punishment for the state and its taxpayers.
Don Bosch, an attorney and legal expert, has handled seven capital punishment cases during his career.
“It’s more expensive to seek the death penalty as a state because of the necessary layers of appeals,” Bosch said. “Remember, death is the one punishment that you can’t correct after implementation.”
Tennessee provides defendants in capital cases with two court-appointed attorneys, compared with one lawyer in other criminal cases.

Capital cases also frequently require costly psychological evaluations and medical testimony. “Those things that require psychologists and medical testimony get very expensive for the state, where those often don’t exist in other types of cases,” Bosch said. Some argue that eliminating or reducing appeals would cut expenses, he added, but doing so would increase the risk of wrongful convictions or executions. “It is the punishment that requires perfection.”
Tennessee has not released updated figures comparing the cost of capital punishment with a life sentence since 2004. Research from states across the country, however, consistently shows that death penalty cases can cost taxpayers several times more than life imprisonment.
“The comptroller has actually been asked over the years, and they’ve never provided that,” Bosch said.
With the court proceedings now complete, however, the most expensive phase of Pike’s case has already passed.
“It probably is going to be pretty close, the cost of imposing the death penalty on Pike, in terms of if she were to stay in prison the rest of her life,” Bosch said.

Pike, 50, was scheduled to be executed by lethal injection at 10 a.m. Wednesday, September 30, at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville for the 1995 murder of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer, 19.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit issued the temporary stay at 8:17 a.m. CDT Wednesday, giving the court additional time to consider a legal challenge raised by Pike’s attorneys. Tennessee then asked the U.S. Supreme Court to vacate the stay and allow the execution to move forward.
The Supreme Court granted Tennessee’s request Wednesday evening. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
The Supreme Court’s decision cleared the way for Tennessee to proceed with the execution but did not resolve the underlying legal claims raised by Pike’s attorneys. As of the latest reports, it had not been confirmed that the execution had actually been carried out.
Pike’s lawyers were seeking to reopen litigation involving her history of childhood sexual abuse and other mitigating evidence. They argued that her trial attorneys failed to adequately investigate and present that history during the sentencing phase of her case.
According to court filings, Pike’s attorneys say she was sexually abused by her grandmother’s boyfriend beginning before preschool and continuing through kindergarten. They also say she was raped by a neighbor at age 11 and by a stranger at age 17.
Her lawyers have also cited a suicide attempt at age 12 and diagnoses of bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. They are seeking to have Pike’s death sentence replaced with a sentence of life imprisonment.
Pike is not denying that she participated in Slemmer’s killing. Prosecutors said Pike and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, tortured and killed Slemmer at a Knoxville Job Corps facility in 1995.
Pike was 18 at the time of the murder, while Shipp was 17. Shipp was convicted for his role in the killing and sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole. He remains incarcerated in Tennessee after being denied parole in October 2025, with his next parole review scheduled for 2031.
Pike was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death. She has remained on Tennessee’s death row since 1996.
The Sixth Circuit’s stay came after a federal district court determined that Pike’s latest filing should be treated as a second or successive habeas petition. Pike challenged that determination, and the appeals court issued the temporary stay while considering whether her claim could proceed.
The state opposed the latest challenge and asked the Supreme Court to lift the stay. Before Wednesday’s temporary halt, the Supreme Court had already denied a separate request from Pike seeking to stop the execution over challenges involving Tennessee’s lethal-injection protocol.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee also denied Pike’s clemency request, leaving the execution scheduled for Wednesday.
The Supreme Court’s order did not explain its reasoning. Justice Sotomayor, joined by Kagan and Jackson, dissented from the decision to vacate the Sixth Circuit’s stay.
If Tennessee carries out the execution, Pike would become the first woman executed by the state in roughly two centuries. She would also be the only person executed by Tennessee in the modern death-penalty era for a crime committed at age 18.
Riverbend Maximum Security Institution is located in Nashville, the Tennessee capital and seat of Davidson County. The prison is in the Cockrill Bend area west of downtown Nashville along the Cumberland River.
